en: The Sūtra on the Parable of the Old City, Spoken by the Buddha.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperially Appointed Court Honorable of the Third Rank, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
Great Master Mingjiao, Dharma-bhadra, in obedience to the Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Bhikṣus! In the past, before I had realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I was dwelling alone in a certain place when a doubt arose in my mind:
‘For what reason do all sentient beings in the world undergo the suffering of saṃsāra?’”
This refers to birth, old age, and death; having ceased, they arise again.
Because those sentient beings do not know this as it truly is, they are unable to escape from the suffering of birth, old age, and death.
"I now reflect: from what cause does this suffering of old age and death arise? By what condition does this old age and death exist?
Having formed this thought, he detached himself from all external dependencies and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed this thoroughly, he then knew it as it truly is:
"Now, this aging and death exist because of birth; furthermore, aging and death exist with birth as their condition.
Having known this dharma, he further reflected:
"By what cause does birth exist, and by what conditions does this phenomenon of birth arise?
Having formed this thought, he detached from all objective supports and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed this thoroughly, he knew it as it truly is:
"Birth arises because of existence; furthermore, with existence as a condition, this phenomenon of birth arises.
Having known this phenomenon, he further reflected:
"What is the cause from which this existence arises, and by what conditions does this phenomenon of existence arise?
Having formed this thought, he detached himself from all objective supports and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed this thoroughly, he then knew it as it truly is:
"Existence arises conditioned by grasping; furthermore, with grasping as a condition, this phenomenon of existence arises.
Having known this phenomenon, he further reflected:
"What cause gives rise to grasping? Furthermore, by what condition does this phenomenon of grasping exist?
Having reflected thus, he detached himself from all objective supports and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed this thoroughly, he then knew it as it truly is:
"Grasping has its cause in craving; furthermore, with craving as a condition, these phenomena of grasping come to be.
Having known this phenomenon, he further reflected:
"From what cause does craving arise, and by what condition does this dharma of craving exist?
Having formed this thought, he detached from all objective supports and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed this thoroughly, he knew it as it truly is:
"Craving has feeling as its cause; furthermore, with feeling as a condition, this phenomenon of craving arises.
Having known this phenomenon, he reflected further:
"What is the cause for the existence of feeling? Furthermore, by what condition does this phenomenon of feeling exist?
Having formed this thought, he detached from all mental distractions and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed this thoroughly, he knew it as it truly is:
"Feeling exists because of contact; furthermore, with contact as a condition, this phenomenon of feeling arises.
Having known this phenomenon, he further reflected:
"What is the cause for the existence of contact? Furthermore, by what conditions does this phenomenon of contact arise?
Having formed this thought, he detached from all objective supports and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed this thoroughly, he then knew it as it truly is:
"Contact exists because of the six sense bases; furthermore, with the six sense bases as a condition, this phenomenon of contact arises.
Having known this phenomenon, he further reflected:
"By what cause do these six sense bases exist now, and by what condition do the phenomena of the six sense bases arise?
Having formed this thought, he detached from all points of reference and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed this thoroughly, he then knew it as it truly is:
"Those six sense bases exist because of name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the phenomenon of the six sense bases comes to be.
Having known this dharma, he further reflected:
"By what cause does this name-and-form exist, and by what condition does this name-and-form arise?
Having formed this thought, he detached from all objective supports and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed this thoroughly, he then knew it as it truly is:
"That name-and-form exists because of consciousness; furthermore, with consciousness as a condition, there is the phenomenon of name-and-form.
Having known this dharma, he further reflected:
"By what cause does consciousness exist, and by what condition does this phenomenon of consciousness arise?
Having formed this thought, he detached from all objective supports and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed this thoroughly, he then knew it as it truly is:
"Such a phenomenon of consciousness exists because of name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form, this phenomenon of consciousness arises.

It is solely through this condition of consciousness that the various formations (*saṃskāra*) are produced. Thus, name-and-form conditions consciousness, consciousness conditions name-and-form, name-and-form conditions the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the six sense bases condition contact (*sparśa*), contact conditions feeling (*vedanā*), feeling conditions craving (*tṛṣṇā*), craving conditions clinging (*upādāna*), clinging conditions becoming (*bhava*), becoming conditions birth (*jāti*), and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair."
"Thus there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
Having understood this Dharma, he further reflected:
"By what cause does one attain the absence of old age and death?"
"By the cessation of what dharma do aging and death cease?
Having formed this thought, he detached from all mental preoccupations and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed with discernment, he came to know it as it truly is:
"If there is no dharma of birth, then there is no aging and death.
When the dharma of birth ceases, aging and death also cease.
Having understood this dharma, he further reflected:
"Which phenomena being absent do the phenomena of birth cease to exist?
Which phenomena having ceased do the phenomena of birth cease?
Having formed this thought, he detached from all mental preoccupations and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed this thoroughly, he then knew it as it truly is:
"If there is no dharma, then there is no dharma of arising.
If a dharma ceases, the dharma of arising also ceases."
“Having understood this dharma, he further reflected:
‘In the absence of what dharma does the dharma of existence not arise?
Upon the cessation of what dharma is the dharma of existence extinguished?’”
Having formed this thought, he detached from all mental preoccupation and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed with discernment, he understood it as it truly is:
"If there is no grasping, then existence itself does not exist."
"When grasping has ceased, existence also ceases.
Having understood this dharma, he further reflected:
"In the absence of what dharma would grasping not exist?"
"By the cessation of which phenomena does the phenomenon of grasping cease?
Having formed this thought, he detached from all mental preoccupation and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed thoroughly, he understood it as it truly is:
"If there is no dharma of craving, there is no dharma of grasping.
When the dharma of craving ceases, the dharma of grasping also ceases.
Having understood this dharma, he further reflected:
"What phenomenon being absent would there be no phenomenon of craving?
With the cessation of what phenomenon does the phenomenon of craving cease?
Having reflected thus, he detached himself from all mental preoccupations and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed this thoroughly, he then knew it as it truly is:
"If the phenomenon of sensation does not exist, the phenomenon of craving does not exist.
When the phenomenon of sensation ceases, the phenomenon of craving also ceases."
"Having understood this dharma, he further reflected:
'In the absence of what dharma does the dharma of feeling not arise?
With the cessation of what dharma does the dharma of feeling cease?'"
Having formed this thought, he detached from all mental preoccupation and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed with discernment, he then knew it as it truly is:
"If the phenomenon of contact does not exist, the phenomenon of feeling does not exist."
“When the phenomenon of contact has ceased, the phenomenon of feeling also ceases.
Having understood this phenomenon, he further reflected:
“In the absence of what phenomenon would the phenomenon of contact not exist?”
"By the cessation of what phenomenon does the phenomenon of contact cease?
Having formed this thought, he detached from all mental objects and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed clearly, he came to know it as it truly is:
"If the six sense bases do not exist, contact does not arise;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact also ceases.
Having understood this teaching, he further reflected:
"Which dharma being absent, do the six sense bases not come to be?
With the cessation of which dharma, do the six sense bases also cease?
Having formed this thought, he became free from all mental distractions and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed this thoroughly, he then knew it as it truly is:
"If name-and-form does not exist, the six sense bases do not come to be;
with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases also cease."
"Having understood this dharma, he further reflected:
'In the absence of what dharma do name-and-form not arise?
With the cessation of what dharma does name-and-form also cease? "
Having formed this thought, he detached from all mental distractions and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed with discernment, he then knew it as it truly is:
"If the phenomenon of consciousness does not exist, name-and-form does not exist."
“When consciousness ceases, name-and-form also ceases.
Having understood this dharma, he further reflected:
“In the absence of what dharma does consciousness cease to exist?”
"Through the cessation of what phenomenon does the phenomenon of consciousness also cease?
Having formed this thought, he detached from all mental preoccupations and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed with discernment, he came to know it as it truly is:
"If the dharma of formations does not exist, the dharma of consciousness does not exist.
If the dharma of formations ceases, the dharma of consciousness also ceases.
Having understood this dharma, he further reflected:
"Which dharma being absent, do the formations (saṃskāra) become absent?
Which dharma having ceased, do the formations cease?
Having formed this thought, he became free from all mental distractions and observed with a concentrated mind.
Having observed this thoroughly, he then knew it as it truly is:
"If ignorance does not exist, the phenomena of volitional formations do not exist.
When ignorance ceases, the phenomena of volitional formations also cease."
Thus, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease;
with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases;
with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease.
With the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases;
with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases.
With the cessation of sensation, craving ceases;
with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases;
with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases.
With the cessation of existence, birth ceases;
with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease.
Thus, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
"Having thoroughly understood each of these dharmas, he further reflected:
'I have now trodden the path traveled by the Buddhas; I have donned the armor worn by those of old; I have reached the city of Nirvana where those of old arrived.'"
The Buddha spoke again, saying: "O Bhikṣus!

It is as if there were a person who wished to travel to a distant place; he would tread upon the path formerly traveled by others, don the armor formerly worn by others, and thus seek out the ancient capital city of those predecessors."
Whether traveling through deep mountains or across vast wildernesses, he journeyed on without ceasing until he reached that ancient city.
The city was vast and expansive; it was the capital where kings of old had resided.
Yet this capital city remains as magnificent and beautiful as ever;
its ponds and gardens are all exceptionally fine,
such that those who behold them never grow weary of or wish to leave them.
Having seen this, the man thought to himself:
"I shall now return to my own country and report this matter in full to the King.
Upon arriving in his native land, he immediately addressed the King, saying:
"Great King, you should know this!
I have donned the armor worn by those of old and tread the path traveled by those of old.
Whether traveling through deep mountains or across vast wildernesses, I proceeded without ceasing until I reached an ancient city."
That city was vast and extensive, being the capital and seat of a former king;
its moats and ramparts remained magnificent as before,
and its ponds, marshes, gardens, and groves were all exceptionally beautiful.
"Whatever people behold, their hearts never grow weary of or abandon it.
Great King, you ought to go there and establish your capital.
Having heard these words, the king immediately granted the petition and, together with his ministers and attendants, soon established his capital in that city.
"And because the king resided there, that capital city became even more magnificent and beautiful; its population flourished, and its abundance and joy were twice what they had been before.
'O Bhikṣus! I am also like this.'"
I tread upon the path formerly traveled by all Buddhas, I don the armor formerly donned by all Buddhas, and I journey toward the ancient city of Nirvāṇa of all Buddhas.
O Bhikṣus!
What is called the ancient path?
What is called the ancient armor?
What is called the ancient city?
This is precisely the Eightfold Noble Path practiced by all Buddhas of the past,
namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
"O Bhikṣus!
This Eightfold Noble Path is the ancient path, the ancient armor, and the ancient city.
It was traversed by previous Buddhas, and I too have followed it; thus one may perceive the origin of old age and death."

Therefore, I have realized the cessation of old age and death, and I have perceived the cessation of birth, becoming, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, and consciousness.
Furthermore, when one contemplates the accumulation of formations, those formations are also brought to cessation;
once the phenomena of formations have ceased, ignorance also ceases;
and once ignorance has ceased, there is nothing further to be contemplated.
At that time, by means of my own supernormal power, I attained perfect enlightenment. "O Bhikṣus!

This True Dharma which I have proclaimed—yours is to apply yourselves with diligence, to train yourselves thus, to practice thus, to keep it in mind and cultivate it, thereby fulfilling the holy life."
Proclaiming the Dharma and its transformation throughout the heavens and among humans, they bring great benefit to sentient beings.
Even bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, brahmins, and non-Buddhist Nirgranthas should likewise practice and proclaim it, bringing great benefit to sentient beings.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this sutra, the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, received it with faith and practiced accordingly.
The Sutra on the Parable of the Old City, Spoken by the Buddha.
